scenes.title: A few seconds at the noticeboard
scenes.description: With the invitations ready, Maya turns to the open day flyer and imagines someone walking past the noticeboard with only a few seconds to look.

scenes.title: The first draft
scenes.description: Maya gives the chat tool who, what, when and where, and a friendly tone. The draft has the right details but opens with a long, formal sentence.

scenes.title: What would you say next?
scenes.description: The learner is asked to choose Maya's next message to the chat tool.

scenes.title: Two more tries
scenes.description: In the same chat, Maya asks the tool to keep the date, time and place and use no more than fifty words, then to sound like she is inviting a neighbour. The third version sounds like her.

scenes.title: A second language
scenes.description: Maya asks for a translated flyer. She cannot check it herself, so a volunteer who speaks the language reads it and changes two words before both versions go up.

scenes.title: Keep the conversation going
scenes.description: If a draft is close, keep the conversation going: say what to keep and what to change, and ask someone who can check what you cannot. The learner thinks about a draft they would like to improve.

cues.text: With the invitations ready, Maya turns to the flyer.
She imagines someone walking past the noticeboard on their way out.
They’ve got a few seconds to see what’s happening and decide if they want to come.
She tells the chat tool who the flyer is for, what’s happening, when and where, and asks for a friendly tone.
The draft comes back with all the right details.
It also starts with, “We are delighted to announce that the community centre will be hosting its forthcoming open day.”
“Nobody’s reading all that on their way out.”
Maya’s about to write it herself.
What would you say to the chat tool next?
Choose Maya’s next message, then carry on.
Maya stays in the same chat.
She types, “Keep the date, time and place. Make it no more than fifty words.”
The new version fits on the flyer.
But there’s still a line about “opportunities for community engagement.”
Maya tries one more time.
“Make it sound like I’m inviting a neighbour.”
This time, it starts with, “Come and see what’s happening at your community centre.”
That sounds like something she’d put on the noticeboard.
Then Maya thinks of the families who’d find the flyer easier to read in another language.
She asks for a translated version.
Since she can’t check the translation herself, she asks a volunteer who speaks the language to read it.
He changes two words that sounded odd.
Then both versions go up.
If a draft is close, you can keep the conversation going.
Tell the tool what to keep and what to change.
And if it gives you something you can’t check yourself, ask someone who can.
Your turn.
Think of a draft you’d like to improve.
What would you type to change its length?
What would you type to change how it sounds?
